newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Cano Limon field loses 1.05 mln barrels output.
newsitem.headline: Cano Limon field loses 1.05 mln barrels output.

text.p: The shut-in at Occidental Petroleum Corp's Cano Limon field, now in its sixth day, has led to a 1.05 million barrel production loss, a spokesman for the state-run oil company Ecopetrol said Tuesday.

At current market prices the lost output would amount to about $20 million. The field was shut-in last Thursday after a spate of leftist rebel attacks, leading Occidental to declare force majeure in the field earlier Tuesday, for the first time since it came on stream.

Ecopetrol, which has a 50 percent stake in the Cano Limon operations, declared force majeure Monday on two crude consignments totaling about 750,000 barrels that had been due for dispatch over the weekend.

But an Ecopetrol spokesman said one of those consignments, about 350,000 barrels, would be substituted with a mixture of crudes drawn from the Central, or Colombia, pipeline. The spokesman conceded, however, that the replacement cargo was of a lower quality than the sweet crude from Cano Limon.
He was unable to give names of the buyers of the cargoes but said they were destined for U.S. refineries around the Gulf.

In a statement issued shortly after it declared force majeure in its Cano Limon, Occidental said: "Occidental rejects the continued terrorist attacks by the guerrillas against the civilian population, the public security forces and the oil infrastructure."

The 300,000 barrels per day capacity pipeline which runs from Cano Limon to the Caribbean coast lifting terminal at Covenas has been out of action since the first rebel dynamite attack on July 6 in eastern Arauca province. It was hit a second time on July 10 -- forcing Occidental to shut in production after it was left without sufficient on-site capacity to store the crude.

Commenting on the situation, Alejandro Martinez, head of the private sector Colombia Oil Companies Association, said the attacks may have negligible impact on world oil prices but would severely dent the country's image in the eyes of potential investors.

"This is a great blow to the Colombian economy and the situation is even more dramatic if we think how it is affecting the image of the country," he said, playing down suggestions that the fragile security situation would force foreign multinationals to quit the country.

Ecopetrol said its repair teams were still unable to get close to the area where the pipleine had been blasted because of a continued rebel presence. President Ernesto Samper, meanwhile, huddled with his Mines and Energy Minister and defense officials to discuss the outlook.
